Kaur v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

2 Nov 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1651Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
The applicant sought leave to appeal from a decision of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Div 2) refusing an extension of time to review a Registrar's summary dismissal of her judicial review application. The underlying Tribunal decision affirmed refusal of a Regional Employer Nomination (subclass 187) visa because her employer's nomination had not been approved. Hill J dismissed the leave application and fixed costs at $5,000.
Key holding

Where a subclass 187 visa criterion requires an approved employer nomination, and the nomination has never been approved and can never now be approved, refusal is the only decision open and leave to appeal will be refused because remittal would be futile.

In this case, as explained, the Tribunal made the only decision that was open to it to make: the Applicant's employer nomination was not approved at the time of the Tribunal's decision, and therefore the 187 visa could not be granted. Further, the Tribunal has refused an application to review the refusal of that employer nomination.

Arias v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

30 Oct 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1903Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
This case concerned two out-of-time judicial review applications by a Colombian citizen challenging ART decisions affirming the cancellation of his Bridging C (Subclass 030) visa and the refusal of his Partner (Temporary) (Subclass 820) visa. The Court refused both extensions of time because the proposed grounds had no reasonable prospects of success and ordered costs in each matter.
Key holding

Under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), an extension of time should be refused where the proposed grounds of judicial review have no prospects of success.

Where there are no prospects of the applicant's grounds of review succeeding, an extension is to be refused.

Naberezhnov and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

28 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2522Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Tribunal reviewed the delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Naberezhnov’s Class BB Subclass 155 visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although he did not pass the character test, the Tribunal was satisfied there was another reason to revoke the cancellation and set aside the review decision.
Key holding

Where an applicant does not pass the character test, the Tribunal must determine whether there is another reason to revoke the mandatory cancellation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), applying Direction No 110.

It follows that the only issue for determination is whether I am satisfied that there is another reason why the visa cancellation decision should be revoked.

Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority

28 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1615Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.
Key holding

Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

27 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2505Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
ZKDP sought review of a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa after a 7-year-6-month drug trafficking sentence. It weighed community protection against ties, rehabilitation, pending charges and other factors in a fact-specific decision.
Key holding

Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

27 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1602Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationCharacter testMigration
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.
Key holding

The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

Before: Leeming JA; Ball JA; Price AJA at [1] Decision: 1. The Tribunal is directed, pur
The NSW Court of Appeal dealt with a notice of motion by the Secretary seeking variations to earlier orders remitting disciplinary proceedings and costs to NCAT. The Court refused to vary the remitter because its scope was already clear, but directed NCAT under cl 29(8)(d) that it may determine the remitted costs of the appeal without being satisfied of special circumstances. Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

23 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1589Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.
Key holding

Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

SRQY and Child Support Registrar (Social security second review)

22 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2480Tribunal reviewVisa nomination
The Tribunal dealt with a child support care percentage dispute after two boys commenced boarding school and a maternal grandfather paid the school fees. It set aside the first review decision and restored the existing 50%/50% care percentage determinations. Key holding

Where the actual care that is taking place corresponds with the existing care percentage, the care percentage determination cannot be revoked under ss 54F or 54H of the Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989.

It further follows that the care that was actually taking place corresponded with the existing care percentage. In these circumstances, the child support law does not permit the existing care percentage determination to be revoked.

Testart v Testart (No 3)

22 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1558Tribunal reviewVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.
Key holding

A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

Riddell v State of Queensland (Department of Education)

22 Oct 2026QIRC[2026] QIRC 338Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewEmployment & workplace
Before: O'Neill IC
The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission allowed Ms Riddell’s public service appeal against a refusal to convert her temporary HP3 Occupational Therapist employment to permanent. The Commission held the refusal was not fair and reasonable because the decision-maker confined the substantially-same-role inquiry to vacant positions, gave inadequate reasons, and treated backfilling/no vacancy as a genuine operational requirement preventing conversion.
Key holding

The absence of a vacant permanent position does not, of itself, amount to a genuine operational requirement preventing conversion of temporary employment to permanent; the decision-maker must focus on the role or a substantially same role.

As has been noted in numerous decisions from the Commission, some of which have been cited above, the lack of a vacant permanent position is not a genuine operational requirement or impediment to the Appellant's temporary employment being converted to permanent. It is expected in this scenario that a position will be created.

BDCN and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review)

21 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2432Tribunal reviewVisa nomination
This was a second review of child support care percentages for two children. The Father alleged the Mother ceased providing care from January 2024 when the family lost its home, with older daughters and friends said to be providing care. The Tribunal found the Mother continued to arrange and provide care, including delegated care, and affirmed the existing 100% care determination to her.
Key holding

A parent’s percentage of care is not reduced merely because care is temporarily delivered through others or because older children assist, where the parent continues to arrange, financially support and meet the children’s needs.

Taking all of the above matters into account, I am not satisfied that the care of the children actually taking place no longer corresponded with the existing percentage of care determination of 100% to the Mother for each of the 2 children.

Hormaza v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

21 Oct 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1925Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationMigration
The applicant sought judicial review of an ART decision affirming refusal of a student visa for failing to meet English language proficiency requirements. He alleged procedural unfairness, his migration agent’s negligence, legal unreasonableness, and the ART’s use of the wrong legislative instrument. The Court dismissed the application, finding no jurisdictional error and that the instrument error was immaterial.
Key holding

A representative’s negligence or administrative error in failing to notify an applicant of a hearing does not, without fraud or dishonesty, vitiate the Tribunal’s decision.

As stated in DUA16 at [15], "an administrative decision [under the Act] is not vitiated merely by bad or negligent advice or some other mishap that leads to detriment to an applicant", including negligence by a representative.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson

20 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1548Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.
Key holding

Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

20 Oct 2026Supreme Court of New South Wales[2026] NSWSC 1288Tribunal reviewVisa nominationCriminal law
Before: Hamill J Decision: (1) The appeal is allowed.(2) The decision of Acting Magistra
This was a NSW Supreme Court appeal against Local Court convictions for a sexual act towards a child and attempted voyeurism. Hamill J allowed the appeal because the Acting Magistrate’s ex tempore reasons were inadequate and failed to address the onus and standard of proof and key exculpatory evidence and submissions. Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

19 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2396Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.
Key holding

A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. I consider that the 'residual' risk of reoffending is acceptable despite the potentially serious consequences for the community, and Mr Hoang's length of residence from a young age must take into account.

This was a second review in a child support matter concerning the parents’ percentage of care for two children after the Mother notified a change of care on 23 March 2024. Lye v Comcare

15 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1517Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationMigration
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.
Key holding

Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

15 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1520Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.
Key holding

Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

Rathore v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

9 Oct 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1990Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
This was an application for judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a student visa for breach of condition 8202(2)(b). The applicant alleged the Tribunal’s discretionary cancellation was legally unreasonable because its reasons did not adequately explain why favourable findings did not outweigh the breach. The Court found no jurisdictional error and dismissed the application.
Key holding

Where a tribunal makes cogent and rational adverse findings and expressly weighs favourable and unfavourable matters, its discretionary cancellation decision is within legal reasonableness and is not affected by jurisdictional error merely because a different outcome might have been open.

The weight attributed to various factors was pre-eminently a matter for the Tribunal subject to the boundaries of legal reasonableness. The concerns raised by the Tribunal were cogent and rational and it was open to the Tribunal to have regard to those matters when considering the weight it placed upon matters which it otherwise found to be in the applicant's favour.

OZY25 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

9 Oct 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1983Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
The applicants sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of Subclass 866 protection visas. They alleged jurisdictional error arising from their former representative’s conduct, which they said caused an uninformed request for a decision on the papers and stultified the statutory review process. The Federal Circuit and Family Court dismissed the application, finding the factual foundation for the alleged stultification was not proved.
Key holding

A claim that representative conduct affected the validity of a Tribunal decision requires proof of the alleged failure and its disabling effect; it cannot be inferred merely from hindsight that a hearing might have offered forensic advantages.

Whatever duties s 56 may impose upon a representative, a failure capable of affecting the validity of the Tribunal's decision must first be proved. Section 56 does not permit the Court to infer deficient advice merely from the fact that, with hindsight, attendance might have offered additional forensic opportunities.

BGS24 sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Protection (Class XA) (Subclass 866) visa. He alleged his former migration agent fraudulently included or altered claims in his protection visa statement without his knowledge or instructions, invalidating the visa application. Key holding

An applicant alleging that a migration agent’s fraud invalidated a visa application bears the onus of distinctly proving the fraud, to the Briginshaw standard, including that the agent acted without the applicant’s knowledge or instructions.

Fraud is a serious allegation that needs to be distinctly made and the burden of proving such an allegation rests with the applicant: SZFDE v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (2007) 232 CLR 189; [2007] HCA 35 at [15] and [38]. The Court must be satisfied that serious allegations of fraudulent conduct have been proved to the level of satisfaction required by Briginshaw v Briginshaw [1938] HCA 34; (1938) 60 CLR 336 at 363 and 368: Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v SZLIX (2008) 245 ALR 501 at [33].

Katyal v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

Le v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

25 Sep 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1864Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
This was a judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Partner (Temporary) (Class UK) visa because the applicant was not satisfied to be the spouse under s 5F of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) and reg 1.15A of the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth). The applicant challenged adverse credibility/reliability findings as arbitrary, irrational and lacking evidentiary foundation, and alleged a failure to consider evidence with an active intellectual process. The Court dismissed the application with costs.
Key holding

Adverse credibility or reliability findings are reviewable for jurisdictional error, but a court will not substitute its own view on the merits where the Tribunal’s findings were reasonably open and its reasoning was not irrational, illogical or otherwise legally unreasonable.

The question is whether the particular reliance on inconsistencies, the findings of implausibility, any assumptions made, or the treatment of corroborative evidence reveal reasoning that is irrational, illogical or otherwise legally unreasonable. If the Tribunal's findings were reasonably open to it, the function of the Court in this matter is not to form its own view on the merits about the reliability of the evidence, including the significance of the inconsistencies, nor the weight to be given to such matters.

EDP25 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

25 Sep 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1863Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
EDP25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of her protection visa. She claimed to be a lesbian who would face harm in Malaysia, but the Tribunal rejected her sexual-orientation claim based on inconsistencies and implausibility. The Court found no jurisdictional error and dismissed the application.
Key holding

Where a tribunal rejects the core factual premise of a protection claim, it need not separately consider whether harm would arise from that rejected premise.

It is well established that a claim may not be expressly considered because it has been subsumed by a finding of greater generality or because the underlying core factual premise has been rejected (see Applicant WAEE v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural and Indigenous Affairs (2003) 236 FCR 593 at [47]). Once the Tribunal rejected the applicant's claim in respect of her sexual orientation, no risk could sensibly be considered to arise from that.

The Tribunal therefore is satisfied that the nature of the applicant's and sponsor's relationship while the sponsor was under eighteen were in the nature of adoption under regs 1.04(1)(c) and (2).

2301755 (Refugee)

24 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2464Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewVisa integrityMigration
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate's refusal to grant a protection visa to a gay man from East Timor who claimed he would face societal and familial harm, including ostracism, forced marriage and employment discrimination, if returned. Accepting his claims as credible and finding that state protection would not be effective, the Tribunal was satisfied he is a refugee under s 36(2)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The decision was set aside and remitted for reconsideration.
Key holding

An applicant cannot be required to conceal or modify his sexual orientation to avoid persecution, and the modification exceptions in s 5J(3) apply where conformity would conflict with a characteristic fundamental to his identity or conceal an innate or immutable characteristic.

I find that the applicant could not take reasonable steps to modify his behaviour to avoid a real chance of persecution. Such modifications would fall within the various exceptions in s 5J(3), including conflicting with a characteristic that is fundamental to the applicant's identity or conscience and concealing an innate or immutable characteristic.

Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security)

22 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2291Tribunal reviewVisa nominationProperty
In Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] ARTA 2291, the Tribunal reviewed a decision reducing Mrs Yerburgh’s age pension by assessing notional income from a farm treated as an unrealisable asset. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the rate for reassessment from 11 October 2024 on the basis that the relevant income amount was her actual annual ordinary income from the farm, not a commercial lease value.
Key holding

Where an unrealisable farm is already being worked commercially to full capacity, the amount reasonably expected from a purely commercial application under s 1130(5)(b) is the actual income from current operations, and the s 1130(5) notional rate is the lesser of that amount and 2.5% of the farm's value.

However, having heard from Mrs Yerburgh, the Tribunal is satisfied that the farm is currently being operated commercially to its full capacity. As such, the Tribunal finds that what Mrs Yerburgh could reasonably be expected to obtain from a purely commercial application of the farm is the income that is actually being generated from its current operations, not some alternative higher commercial lease figure as adopted by Centrelink.

Key holding

Where a claimant holds a medical certificate exempting them from mutual obligation requirements for the relevant period, and Centrelink's delay in recording that exemption (combined with a failure to notify the plan requirement) puts compliance beyond the claimant's control, the claimant is not required to satisfy the employment pathway plan requirements and payment remains payable.

8 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2445Tribunal reviewVisa nominationProperty
The Tribunal reviewed Centrelink’s rejection of Ms Ludlam’s jobseeker payment claim because her combined assets exceeded the applicable limit. Centrelink treated the Cairns house as her principal home and as an asset, applying the lower homeowner assets limit. The Tribunal found Ms Ludlam was not a homeowner and remitted the claim for reassessment under the higher non-homeowner limit.
Key holding

Where a person leaves their owned home and resides in rented accommodation without an s 11A circumstance preserving it as the principal home, the person is not a homeowner under s 11(4) and the non-homeowner assets limit applies, although the former home may still be counted as an asset.

The Cairns property ceased to be Ms Ludlam's principal home when she left Cairns and took up residence in rented accommodation in Canberra. She therefore was not a homeowner as defined in subsection 11(4) of the Act and the higher asset limit applies.

Even where a conviction ground for cancellation under s 116(1)(g) is established, the Tribunal may decline to cancel a temporary spouse visa where the best interests of affected children and associated family hardship outweigh the seriousness of the offending in the particular circumstances.

Spaleta v Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] FCAFC 5 (11 February 2026)

11 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 5Tribunal reviewVisa nomination
This was a Full Court appeal about a disability support pension claim. The appellant challenged the AAT’s finding that her conditions were not fully treated or stabilised, so she could not get 20 impairment points under s 94(1)(b) of the Social Security Act 1991 (Cth). The Full Court allowed the appeal, holding that “reasonable treatment” under the Impairment Tables Determination requires consideration of whether treatment is affordable to the claimant, and remitted the matter.
Key holding

In assessing whether treatment is “reasonable treatment” under s 6(7) of the Impairment Tables Determination, “reasonable cost” requires consideration of whether the treatment is reasonably affordable to the claimant in their circumstances, not merely whether the cost is objectively reasonable in the market.

A question arises as to whether the reference to "reasonable cost" in s 6(7)(b) is to the objective reasonableness of the cost of the treatment, or to the different question whether the treatment is reasonably affordable to a claimant in the position of the person concerned. In our view, the latter is the better construction having regard to the context and purpose of the provision.

Sukhwinder Singh (Migration)

10 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4024Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Alan McMurran
Mr Sukhwinder Singh applied for a Subclass 494 Skilled Employer Sponsored Regional (Provisional) visa based on a nomination by Lawson Chinese Pty Ltd. The delegate refused the visa because there was no approved nomination, and the sponsor later withdrew its review of the nomination refusal. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because the applicant could not satisfy the mandatory approved-nomination criterion.
Key holding

For a Subclass 494 visa, the mandatory cl 494.213 criterion is not met where the nomination identified in the application has not been approved under s 140GB, so the refusal must be affirmed.

The Tribunal finds therefore that cl 494.213 is not met and the Department decision must be affirmed.

Sadh (Migration)

8 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4051Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Christine Cody
The Tribunal considered an application to review a delegate’s refusal of a Visitor (Class FA) (Subclass 600) tourist stream visa. The visa applicant had applied offshore and there was no relevant sponsorship, nomination or included relative particulars. The Tribunal found the refusal was not a reviewable decision and it had no jurisdiction.
Key holding

The Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to review a visitor visa refusal where the decision does not satisfy any reviewable-decision category under the Migration Act, including because the applicant was offshore and no relevant sponsorship, nomination or relative particulars existed.

As the delegate's decision is not reviewable under Parts 5 or 7 of the Act it follows that the application for review was not properly made and the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction in this matter.

Rangiuia and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Migration)

8 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3550Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Tribunal reviewed the cancellation of Mr Rangiuia’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). He conceded that he did not pass the character test under s 501(6)(b) because of his membership of the Mongrel Mob and Bandidos outlaw motorcycle gangs. The Tribunal affirmed cancellation, finding protection of the Australian community and serious family violence outweighed his ties to Australia and the best interests of his children.
Key holding

Once a non-citizen fails the character test, the Tribunal’s remaining task is to exercise the s 501(2) cancellation discretion in accordance with Direction No. 110.

Having failed the character test, the issue for the Tribunal is whether to exercise the discretion to cancel the visa, guided by the considerations set out in Direction 110.

2320261 (Refugee)

4 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4442Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Jessica Edis
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of a protection visa to a Zambian man who claimed he feared harm because he and his family suspected his father, a former senior Zambian official, was poisoned and that associates died suspiciously. The Tribunal accepted the applicant was sincere but found his claims speculative and not Convention-related, with no real risk of significant harm. It nevertheless recommended Ministerial intervention under s 417 due to strong compassionate circumstances affecting his Australian wife and child.
Key holding

For the refugee criterion, an applicant must show the feared persecution is linked to a s 5J(1)(a) Convention reason; a uniquely personal fear without that nexus cannot satisfy s 36(2)(a).

He has never suggested (nor is there any evidence which suggests) that his fear is linked to any one or more of the reasons set out in s 5J(1)(a).

Binti Hussin (Migration)

Before: Suseela Durvasula
Mrs Suzi Binti Hussin sought review of a decision refusing her Electronic Travel Authority (Class UD) visa, Subclass 601. The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction because an ETA refusal is not a reviewable decision under the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The review application was therefore not properly made and could not proceed to merits review.
Key holding

A refusal of an Electronic Travel Authority (Class UD) visa is not reviewable by the Tribunal, so the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction over an application seeking review of such a refusal.

Decisions to refuse to grant an ETA are not reviewable by the Tribunal because they are applied for while the applicant is outside the migration zone or in immigration clearance, and do not include a criterion for a relevant sponsorship or visiting a relative.

The Hour Glass (Australia) Pty Ltd sought review of a delegate’s refusal to approve a nomination for a Subclass 482 visa in the Short-term stream. Key holding

A refusal of a Training (Subclass 407) visa is reviewable only if, at the time of the review application, the applicant has an approved sponsor nomination or has a pending review of the nomination refusal.

A migration review application is not valid, and the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction, where the prescribed fee has not been paid within the prescribed period or any applicable reasonable period after a hardship-reduction determination.

The applicant sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming the refusal of a Student (Subclass 500) visa because he did not satisfy the genuine temporary entrant criterion in cl 500.212. The Court held that, having found cl 500.212(a) was not met, the Tribunal was not required to consider sub-clause (b), that no clearly articulated hardship claim was made, and that the Tribunal properly applied Direction No. 69 without treating it as a checklist. No jurisdictional error was found and the application was dismissed with costs.

The applicant's parent visa was refused on character grounds under s 501, which by operation of s 501F automatically cancelled his bridging visa and led to his immigration detention.
